title: State Department Proposes Sweeping New Compliance Rules for J-1 Visa Holders
excerpt: The proposed regulations would consolidate status requirements, expand termination grounds, and impose heavier monitoring duties on program sponsors — adding to growing pressure on Indian researchers and doctors in the US.
body:
• The US Department of State has proposed a rule that would consolidate and tighten compliance requirements for J-1 exchange visitors, expanding the grounds on which participation can be terminated.
  • The proposal follows a separate DHS rule, effective September 15, that ends the decades-old "duration of status" system and caps J-1 admissions at four years.
  • Over 12,000 J-1 visas were issued to Indian nationals in fiscal year 2024, covering postdoctoral researchers, medical residents, professors, and trainees.
  • Program sponsors — universities, research institutions, and teaching hospitals — would face heavier monitoring and reporting obligations under the proposed rule.

The US Department of State (DOS) has published a proposed rule in the Federal Register that would significantly overhaul how exchange visitors on J-1 visas maintain their legal status, broadening the government's authority to terminate participation and placing new compliance burdens on the institutions that sponsor them.

The proposed regulation lands just weeks after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) finalized a separate, related rule ending the long-standing "duration of status" (D/S) framework for J-1, F-1, and I visa holders. That rule, set to take effect on September 15, replaces open-ended stays with fixed admission periods of up to four years — a change that has already drawn sharp criticism from medical associations and universities.

What the Proposed Rule Changes

The DOS proposal does not alter who qualifies for a J-1 visa. Instead, it targets what happens after arrival. For the first time, the regulations would consolidate the scattered requirements for maintaining exchange visitor status into a single, unified framework. Under the current system, rules governing an exchange visitor's status are spread across different regulatory provisions, creating ambiguity about when someone may fall out of status.

The proposed rule lays out specific scenarios that constitute a "failure to maintain exchange visitor status," including unauthorized employment, failure to meet program requirements, and overstaying the authorized program period. It also expands the grounds on which DOS can terminate an individual's participation in the Exchange Visitor Program, adding reasons such as criminal conduct, fraud or misrepresentation, and national security concerns.

For exchange visitors who do fall out of status, the rule would formally codify a reinstatement process. While reinstatement has historically been available through informal administrative practice, the proposed regulation would establish detailed eligibility criteria, documentation requirements, and procedures for the first time — a move DOS says will bring transparency and consistency to a previously ad hoc system.

Heavier Burden on Sponsors

The proposed rule also shifts substantial responsibility onto designated program sponsors — the universities, research institutions, and teaching hospitals that administer J-1 programs. Sponsors would be required to monitor participants more closely, promptly report events that affect an exchange visitor's eligibility, and maintain accurate records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), the joint DHS-DOS database.

Sponsors would also be required to terminate participants who provide false or incomplete information during the application process or during their program. A new formal process would allow exchange visitors to challenge termination decisions — a procedural safeguard that does not currently exist in the regulations.

"It forces scientists to prove the necessity of their stay to a bureaucrat rather than a university, turning research timing into a discretionary government decision."

— Mary E. Walsh, Immigration Attorney, Iandoli, Desai & Cronin

12,000 Indian J-1 Holders in the Crosshairs

The J-1 visa is one of the most widely used pathways for Indian nationals entering US academia and healthcare. According to State Department data, over 12,000 J-1 visas were issued to Indian citizens in fiscal year 2024. The visa is used extensively by Indian postdoctoral researchers, scientists, university professors, and medical professionals undergoing residency or fellowship training at US institutions.

India is the largest source of international STEM talent for the United States, and Indian nationals have experienced some of the steepest declines in visa issuance amid the broader tightening. F-1 student visa issuances fell 36% during the critical summer months of 2025, according to an analysis of State Department data by the Chronicle of Higher Education, while J-1 visa issuances dropped 13% in May 2025 alone.

The cumulative effect of multiple rule changes — the end of duration of status, stricter compliance requirements, a $100,000 fee on H-1B applications for candidates outside the US, and a wage-weighted H-1B lottery system — is creating what Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, described as an unprecedented crisis.

"In my 37 years of being in this field, I have never seen such a perfect storm."

— Fanta Aw, CEO, NAFSA: Association of International Educators

Healthcare Workforce at Risk

The stakes extend well beyond immigration paperwork. About one in 10 physicians in US residency and fellowship programs train under a J visa. Nearly 17,500 J-1 physicians were sponsored by Intealth, the organization that administers J-1 physician visas, in 2025 — working at nearly 780 teaching hospitals across the country. That figure represents a 76% increase over the past decade.

A Health Affairs study published this month found that reliance on J-1 physician trainees is highest in states already facing severe physician shortages: North Dakota (29% of all physicians-in-training), Connecticut (17%), and West Virginia (17%). Regions including the Upper Midwest, Northern Plains, and Appalachia depend on these trainees to sustain medical services where physician recruitment is most challenging.

Medical associations have been vocal in opposing the broader J-1 overhaul. The Association of American Medical Colleges said in a statement that ending duration of status "does not take into account the breadth of complexities of graduate, postdoctoral, and medical residency programs, many of which often take longer than four years to complete."

What's Next

The DOS proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days before it can be finalized. The separate DHS rule ending duration of status is already finalized and set to take effect on September 15, 2026. Together, the two regulations represent the most significant restructuring of the J-1 Exchange Visitor Program in decades — and Indian researchers, doctors, and trainees planning US stints will need to track both closely.
nri_angle: Over 12,000 Indian nationals receive J-1 visas annually for research, medical training, and academic exchange, making them among the most directly affected by the proposed compliance overhaul.
